A Mumbai infrastructure contractor is raising working capital through an SME IPO. Here is what its DRHP tells you — and what it does not.

beats.beat: The business splits into two segments: creation of infrastructure and operation of a ready-mix concrete plant. Infrastructure work spans railways, bridges and roadways — platforms, station buildings, gauge conversion, track-laying, multiple bridge types, and bituminous and concrete roads.

Revenue is won through a disclosed tender process: the client floats a tender, the contractor bids, the lowest quote gets a Letter of Acceptance, the contractor deposits a performance guarantee, and then the site is handed over for execution.
The concrete side operates a state-of-the-art RMC plant at Kashimira in Thane district, with investments in machines and quality-control systems.

Major customers named in the filing are almost all public-sector: Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai, Western Railway, Central Railway, Mumbai Railway Vikas Corporation Ltd, Mumbai Metropolitan Region Development Authority, Dedicated Freight Corridor Corporation, plus Sky Way Infrastructure, Dev Engineers, GCC Hotel and Krypton Corp.

The client list is narrow at the top. Western Railway has been a client since 2006 and contributes 52% of the orders on hand; the top customers together contributed 57% of revenue for the year ended March 31, 2018.

The company's own strengths list is conventional — cost efficiency, timely delivery, technical expertise, quality, transparency — but it does disclose a specific technique: 'box pushing' for project execution, and leadership with more than 20 years' infrastructure industry experience.
The filing says the order book is strong, but the only order-book figure in the extract is the Western Railway concentration; no absolute order-book value is disclosed in these pages.

beats.beat: The restated statements run from FY2014 to FY2018. Revenue has fallen in four straight years: from ₹90.21 crore in FY2015 to ₹60.53 crore in FY2018, with ₹73.44 crore in FY2017 and ₹74.53 crore in FY2016.
Profit after tax tells a different shape: it fell from ₹0.96 crore in FY2014 to ₹0.16 crore in FY2017, then jumped to ₹3.15 crore in FY2018 — a spike worth reading alongside the revenue decline.

Profit before interest, depreciation and tax (PBDIT, the closest disclosed proxy to EBITDA) was ₹9.29 crore in FY2018, up from ₹6.76 crore in FY2017; earlier years were ₹7.83 crore (FY2016), ₹9.46 crore (FY2015) and ₹7.84 crore (FY2014).

The balance sheet is working-capital heavy: total assets of ₹82.32 crore as on March 31, 2018, with short-term borrowings of ₹35.37 crore dwarfing long-term borrowings of ₹1.33 crore. Short-term debt has risen from ₹30.82 crore in FY2014.
The filing discloses negative cash flow in recent years but the extract does not include the cash-flow statement figures, so the depth of that negative flow is not quantified here.

The basis-for-issue-price section reports per-share metrics for FY2016-FY2018: FY2018 EPS of 12.59 and NAV per share of 28.14 are among the disclosed values, with FY2016 and FY2017 figures materially lower.

beats.beat: Amit Bholanath Mishra is the promoter and managing director, holding 74,95,476 equity shares — 90.949% of pre-issue paid-up equity share capital. His PAN is disclosed in the filing.

Three whole-time directors — Bharat Kumar Parmar, Shree Prakash Singh and Mukesh Pandey — each hold 300 equity shares. The CFO is Anchal Pachori, 28, a chartered accountant, and the company secretary and compliance officer is Mohit Soni, 26. Hatim Sakerwala holds 9% of the equity.
The filing makes clean legal statements: none of the directors is on the RBI list of wilful defaulters, and no criminal cases have been filed against the directors.

Related-party transactions are disclosed: a loan of ₹68.4 lakh taken from KMP/board members in FY2018, director remuneration of ₹57.7 lakh in FY2018, and outstanding payables to related parties of ₹324.3 lakh as on March 31, 2018.

Governance flags are material: two promoter-promoted companies — Al-Noor Chickens Private Limited and A B Magma Automobiles Private Limited — were struck off by the Registrar of Companies in March 2016 for non-operation. The company also disclosed that it issued equity shares in the last 12 months at a price that may be lower than the issue price.

beats.beat: This is the infrastructure and construction sector — power, bridges, dams, roads and urban infrastructure — described by the filing as highly fragmented and working-capital intensive, contributing roughly 8% to India's GDP at constant prices.

The demand drivers the filing cites are government-led: flagship programmes including 100 Smart Cities Mission, AMRUT, Make in India and Power for All; eased FDI norms in 15 sectors including real estate and construction; and rising industrialisation, urbanisation, disposable income and population.

The market-size numbers in the filing: India requires investment worth ₹50 trillion in infrastructure by 2022; the construction market was about US$400 billion in 2015 heading toward US$1,000 billion by 2025; the logistics sector is expected to grow from US$160 billion in 2017 to US$215 billion by 2020 at a 10.5% CAGR.

Macro tailwinds disclosed: India's GDP growth above 7% in 2017; cumulative growth of 4.2% in eight core industries in 2017-18; India jumped 19 places in the World Bank Logistics Performance Index 2016 to rank 35th; working-age population expected to rise to 64% by 2021.
Competition is both organised and unorganised, and the filing's own SWOT names three headwinds: slow pace of government projects, working-capital crunch, and changes in government policies.

beats.beat: A B Infrabuild is a Mumbai-area infrastructure contractor with two lines of work: building railway, bridge and road projects, and running a ready-mix concrete plant. It is raising money through an issue of 44,28,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at a price yet to be fixed.
The filing's stated purpose for the money is company-side — working capital of ₹1,130 lakh and general corporate purposes — with no offer-for-sale seller named in the extract.

The company's restated numbers tell a split picture: revenue has fallen for four straight years while FY2018 profit jumped. This report walks through the business, the offer, the numbers and the risks the DRHP itself names.

intro.purpose: Orient the reader in one breath: who A B Infrabuild is, what it does, and what it is selling in this IPO.

beats.beat: The issue is 44,28,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at an issue price to be determined — the lead manager is Mark Corporate Advisors Private Limited and the registrar is Bigshare Services Private Limited.

The extract lists only 'Equity Shares Offered' — 44,28,000 shares — and does not disclose a separate offer-for-sale component or name a selling shareholder. The use of proceeds, however, is company-side: ₹1,130 lakh for working capital requirements and an undisclosed amount for general corporate purposes.

The filing concedes governance constraints on the money: no independent agency was appointed to appraise the proposed project, and no monitoring agency has been named — deployment of funds is at the discretion of management and the board, though monitored by the audit committee.

beats.beat: Railway concentration: Indian Railways is the largest customer, contributing 57% of revenue in Fiscal 2018, and Western Railway alone is 52% of the order book. The filing says losing that customer would cause a significant dip in revenues.
Tender dependence: revenue depends on government and government-department acceptance of bids; if most bids are not accepted, or the company negotiates a lower bid value, performance suffers.

Negative cash flow: the filing says the company had negative cash flow in recent financial years and warns that sustained negative cash flow could materially harm the business, financial condition and results of operations.
On-demand unsecured loans: the company had ₹405.02 lakh of unsecured loans as on March 31, 2018, repayable on demand; any repayment call could hurt cash flow and financial condition.

Promoter history: two companies promoted by the promoter were struck off by the Registrar of Companies in March 2016 for non-operation — a specific governance flag a prospective investor would want to weigh.

beats.beat: The DRHP's basis-for-issue-price section compares the company's accounting ratios with a peer group, but the extract gives only two raw numbers from that page — 12.39 and 44.71 — without naming the peers or labelling which ratio is which.
The issue price itself is still shown as [●]; the filing says the price will be justified by the accounting ratios, and that the issue price will be some multiple of the ₹10 face value.

Because the peer names and column labels are not in the extract, this report will present exactly what is disclosed — the company's own FY2016-FY2018 per-share and ratio metrics, plus the two unlabelled peer-comparison values — rather than manufacture an implied price range.
